title: Outliers
author: Malcolm Gladwell
blurb: Malcolm Gladwell challenges the myth of the self-made genius. He argues that extraordinary achievers, the outliers, owe their success to more than brains and hard work. In the first half, he looks at opportunity. A birth month can decide a hockey career. Thousands of hours of practice separate experts from amateurs. Being born in the right year can open doors that stay shut for everyone else. In the second half, he turns to cultural legacy. Attitudes passed down for generations shape how we argue and how we handle risk. They even shape how pilots speak in a cockpit, and how hard students work at math. Gladwell's point is hopeful. If success comes from opportunities and environments, then we can deliberately build better ones and give far more people a real chance to excel.

lessons.b: The surprising health of one small Pennsylvania town shows that success and wellbeing often come from community and context, not just individual choices.
Small early advantages, like being born just after an age cutoff, snowball over time into big differences in who succeeds.
True mastery takes roughly 10,000 hours of practice, and the people who get there usually had rare chances to put in those hours.
